The agreement with France has redrawn the frontier and opened a new phase of union in central Italy. Ministers now face the work of reconciling the new provinces with the kingdom, while the surrender of Nice and Savoy divides patriotic opinion.

Garibaldi has established an expeditionary government in Sicily. His advance offers an opening for Italian union, but an independent revolutionary command may outrun royal diplomacy. Turin can allow discreet cooperation or insist on keeping its distance.

The crown now possesses Perugia and Ancona, while Rome remains beyond its administration. The new provinces provide a link between northern and southern Italy, but their incorporation has sharpened the dispute with the Papacy.

Commission a survey of local laws, offices and public obligations in the newly united kingdom. Reconciling their records will take time, but offers a basis for a common civil administration.

The commission has completed its survey of the new provinces. Ministers now possess a common account of offices and obligations from which to administer the kingdom. The settlement does not erase local grievances or settle the wider southern question.

Rome remains under Papal rule. Deputies can affirm it as the national aspiration, accepting friction with the Pope and France, or concentrate on consolidating the kingdom already united. A parliamentary declaration cannot itself change possession of the city.
